newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices slip as US government monitors supplies.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices slip as US government monitors supplies.

text.p: Oil prices slipped for the second day in succession on Thursday, prompting some speculation that a startling rally might have peaked, for the time being at least.
London December futures for international benchmark Brent crude traded down 14 cents at $23.80 a barrel.
Brent for November earlier this week broke $25 for the first time in nearly six years in a scare over a possible shortage of heating oil supplies in the West this winter.
Talk that the U.S. government might intervene to protect heating oil consumers this winter, possibly by encouraging a clampdown on exports, had helped undermine prices, dealers said.
High European prices have allowed traders to make money by selling more than a million tonnes of heating oil from U.S. markets to European buyers over the past two months.
The exports have exacerbated U.S. inventory shortfalls, running 40 percent down on last year in the key northeast region and 10 percent below normal across the whole country.

U.S. oil company executives will meet U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary and a Justice Department representative on Friday to discuss what can be done to ensure low heating oil stocks don't hit consumers too hard this winter.
"What is spooking some people is this meeting on Friday," said Gerry Samuels, an analyst at U.S. Arb Oil.
Though the Energy Department has said it will not intervene in the market, there has been persistent speculation among traders that companies may volunteer action.
Exxon Corp is rumoured to have told clients that it will stop or at least curtail exports of distillates. The company declined to comment.
Dealers were divided on Thursday on whether oil markets had merely paused for breath before resuming their rise, or whether prices might be set for a heavier tumble.
Some saw signs of market fatigue after the bull run which carried crude up 40 percent in just four months.
"It's too high. I don't think the fundamentals can support prices at these levels," said a London-based trader.
"Every time this market seems ready for a substantial correction it bounces back again," said another.
